## 4. Discussion

In this study, serum samples collected from the HIV Confirmatory
Laboratory of Meizhou People's Hospital Medical Laboratory Center (From
May 2008 to December 2019) were analyzed. Primary HIV screening by ELISA
or CLIA revealed HIV-positive rates of 0.11% and 1.94%, respectively.
ELISA and CLIA are simple and high-throughput; however, they are
associated with relatively high false-positive outcomes (Liu and Jiang,
2004; Chen, 2012; Wu et al., 2018). More rigorous strategies, such as
western blotting, are needed for verification. Herein, 195 samples were
confirmed as HIV-1 positive by western blotting, with no HIV-2 positive
samples being observed. Most HIV-1 infected patients were determined to
be in the middle and AIDS stages of the infection (Supplementary Table
S1), and there were more men than women patients (Table 1). The HIV-1
infected patients are mainly farmers and migrant workers (Table 1), whose
education level is generally low, and who may have less knowledge about
AIDS prevention. It is particularly important to further enhance the
coverage of AIDS prevention knowledge in the rural population. The highest
detection rate of HIV-infected was in July (Figure 1); nonetheless, the
reason behind this observation remains to be further investigated. A
contemporaneous comparison of HIV-diagnosed cases in 2018 and 2019
suggested an increasing trend in Meizhou (Figure 1). Therefore, HIV
prevention and control in the Meizhou community cannot be relaxed. It is
necessary to further improve the coverage of HIV screening to achieve
early detection and treatment. WB is the gold standard for confirming HIV
infection and provides information on virus and host responses. The full
WB pattern contains 10 bands that are specific to HIV-1. However, the
band patterns of WB vary according to stages of the infection, prevalent
viral strains, and cohorts, thus displaying significant regional
characteristics. In this study, we observed 30 types of WB patterns from
the 195 HIV-positive samples (Table 2). Reactivity with seven bands (p24,
p31, gp41, p51, p66, gp120, and gp160) was the most commonly observed
pattern with a proportion of 28.21%, while the complete 10-band pattern
occurred in only 9.74% of the samples, which was different from other
studies that reported the full pattern as the main outcome (Sudha et al.,
2006). Envelope protein bands (gp160, gp120, and gp41), pol protein (p66),
and gag protein (p24) were the most prevalent, which was consistent with
the previous studies (Zhong et al., 2012; Xie and Chen, 2018). p55, p39,
and p17 were the most frequently missing bands (Figure 2). The frequencies
of p55 and p39 bands were low in samples from every infection stage
(Table 3), but the p17 bands were only significantly lower in cases at
the AIDS and middle stages of the infection (Table 3). These results
indicated that lack of antibody reactivity to p17 was associated with
disease progression. HAART is the most effective clinical treatment for
AIDS (Sattwika et al., 2023). In Meizhou, TDF/AZT +3TC+EFV/NVP is the
most commonly adopted initial treatment regimen, with the EFV+AZT/3TC
regimen being less prescribed. Based on the drug-resistant genotype assay
results, the main resistant HIV-1 strains in Meizhou were the CRF01-AE
subtype, followed by the CRF07-BC subtype, which is consistent with the
current situation in China (Huo et al., 2019). In Meizhou, the
resistance mutation of NNRTIs is the most prevalent, followed by that of
NRTIs. Moreover, the cross-resistance of NRTIs and NNRTIs co-occurred in
patients and accounted for 40.54% of drug-resistant mutations, indicating
that multidrug resistance is widespread in the region. This may be
related to the long-term use of first-line therapeutic drugs, resulting in
the continuous accumulation of cross-drug-resistant mutant HIV-1 strains
(Ma et al., 2010). Studies have shown that the accumulation of
thymidine analogue-resistant mutations causes almost all NRTI resistance
(Zha and Zha, 2006). In the resistance mutations of NRTIs, the M184V
mutation was most prevalent, followed by K65R (Table 4). It has been
reported that the M184V mutation causes significant resistance to 3TC but
increases the sensitivity to TDF and AZT (Zuo, 2020). The K65R mutation
was reported to produce moderate or high resistance to TDF and ABC (Guo,
2014). In this study, we observed that some patients simultaneously
harboured mutations at the K65R and M184V sites; however, treatment with
AZT was still appropriate, indicating that the first-line treatment
regimen was efficacious for patients in Meizhou with this drug-resistant
form of the disease. These results may explain why the HIV antiviral
treatment failure ratio due to resistant mutations in Meizhou (8.95%)
was much lower than the global data (40.30%--84.00%) (Shen and Su, 2019).
Compared with the high incidence of drug-resistant mutations in NRTIs and
NNRTIs, resistant mutations in PIs were only found in one out of the 37
cases (Table 4). These results suggest that patients in Meizhou with
drug-resistant HIV/AIDS may still be sensitive to PIs since resistance
mutations rarely occur in response to this group of drugs. Therefore, when
patients develop cross-resistance to NRTIs and NNRTIs simultaneously and
the first-line treatment regimen ceases to be efficacious, second-line
treatment may be adopted. The study of clinical and epidemiological
characteristics of HIV patients is conducive to the establishment of
regional HIV transmission and epidemic identification standards and early
warning systems. At the same time, the correlation between serological
characteristics and clinical drug resistance was analyzed to provide useful
information for clinical timely acquisition of HIV biological information
and prediction of drug resistance (Shchemelev et al., 2023). The analysis
model of the correlation between serotype and drug resistance may provide
new ideas for HIV epidemic prevention and identification analysis. By
studying the laboratory diagnosis and monitoring indicators and drug
resistance of HIV infected people in Meizhou city, we provide scientific
clinical basis for AIDS prevention and treatment. Although the detection
methods of HIV infection are becoming more and more mature and
diversified, there are still some problems that need to be studied and
solved. One of the prominent problems is the long incubation period of
HIV-infected people and the different window periods of HIV detection
methods. We combine the characteristics of the regional HIV epidemic in
the detection population and adopt appropriate detection methods to reduce
the missed detection rate of HIV-infected people. In the process of
antiretroviral drug treatment, clinical laboratory detection of drug
resistance genes appears in various problems, we need to further explore,
such as how long the interval of drug resistance monitoring detection is
appropriate, can timely understand the characteristics of HIV antiviral
resistance, is conducive to HIV infected people to develop effective
treatment plans.

## 5. Conclusion

In summary, we explored the characteristics of clinical HIV infection in
Meizhou, China, by retrospectively analyzing samples from HIV-infected
people obtained from May 2008 to December 2019. Most of the 195 positive
cases were found to be male and, in the middle, and AIDS stages. They
were mainly from groups with relatively lower education levels. We found
that the most prevalent pattern was reactivity with seven bands (p24,
p31, gp41, p51, p66, gp120, and gp160), instead of the full-band
pattern reported in other regions. The WB bands including p55, p39, and
p17 were the most frequently missing bands. We further observed decreased
detection of the p17 antibody in patients in the middle to the AIDS stage
of the infection/disease. Most resistant mutations were related to NRTIs
and NNRTIs; only one case carried a mutation resistant to PIs, suggesting
the presence of protease inhibitors in the treatment regimen will work
better in local patients. Our data described the specific epidemiological
patterns, serum antibody profiles and drug resistance genotypes of HIV-infected
patients in Meizhou, and are of great significance for guiding local
treatment strategies in the future.

According to DREAM protocols, individuals with virological failure were enrolled in a six-month enhanced adherence support program; no ART regimen changes are made during the enhanced adherence support phase. A repeated viral load test was performed after this period, and those with persistent viremia ( \(>1000\) copies/mL) were eligible for genotypic resistance testing. Only individuals on DTG-containing regimens at the time of resistance testing were included in this analysis. Elsewhere we described the wider population of the individuals with elevated VL [9]. Inclusion criteria were: (i) confirmed HIV-positive status; (ii) being on a DTG-based regimen at the time of resistance testing; (iii) confirmed virological failure (HIV RNA \(>1000\) copies/mL) after at least six months of enhanced adherence support. Exclusion criteria included: (i) switching from DTG to another regimen before resistance testing; (ii) insufficient plasma samples for sequencing; or (iii) incomplete clinical records. Due to the retrospective nature of the study and limitations in documentation, we were unable to determine the exact number of eligible individuals who did not undergo resistance testing. Genotypic testing was requested at the discretion of the treating clinicians, based on clinical judgment and operational feasibility. However, specific criteria guiding these decisions were not systematically recorded or analyzed. Logistical constraints such as reagent availability, sample transport, and staffing likely also contributed to the limited number of tests performed; hence, only a subset of eligible individuals underwent resistance testing. ### Resistance testing procedures Resistance testing followed standardized DREAM protocols. Plasma samples from participants with confirmed virological failure were collected and sent to the Zimpeto DREAM laboratory, where viral RNA was extracted and amplified using an in-house reverse transcription and nested PCR method. Sequencing of the HIV integrase region was performed using the Sanger method at INQABA Biotechnical Industries, South Africa. Sequences were analyzed and interpreted directly at INQABA using the Stanford HIV Drug Resistance Database. DTG resistance was classified according to Stanford penalty scores as follows: susceptible (score \(< 10\) ) (S), low-level resistance (10-14) (LLR), intermediate resistance (15-29) (IR), and high-level resistance \((\geq 30)\) (HLR). Resistance mutations were identified in the integrase region, and, when available, in the reverse transcriptase and protease regions. ### Data collection and variables Clinical and demographic data were extracted from the DREAM electronic medical records. Variables collected included age, sex, duration on ART, number of prior ART regimens, HIV-1 subtype (when available), and reason for initiating DTG (first-line, switch while suppressed, or switch after failure). Resistance to DTG was classified using Stanford scoring. ### Statistical analysis Descriptive statistics were used to summarize baseline characteristics. Categorical variables were presented as frequencies and percentages, and continuous variables as medians with interquartile ranges (IQR). ### Ethics The study was approved by the National Bioethics Committee for Health of Mozambique (Ref: 430/CNBS/24, July 19, 2024). Given the retrospective nature of the study and the use of routinely collected anonymized data, the requirement for informed consent was waived. The study was conducted in accordance with the principles of the Declaration of Helsinki and relevant national guidelines. ## Results ### Study population and baseline characteristics In the considered period, 28 individuals on DTG-based ART who underwent resistance testing following confirmed virological failure (HIV RNA \(\geq 1000\) copies/mL) after six months of enhanced adherence support were included in the analysis. In our previous study, we reported a suppression control rate among patient on DTG-based treatment very high (95%), which clearly demonstrates the success of such regimens; however, a growing body of literature is showing also the potential risk of the emergence of DTG-resistance in the African continent. Although the percentage of resistance remains relatively low, it could still translate into thousands of affected patients across the region. In large randomized studies such as the NADIA trial (Uganda, Kenya, Zimbabwe) and the DAWNING trial, the rate of INSTI resistance emergence remained low (4% and 1%, respectively), thanks to intensive viral load monitoring and optimized therapeutic strategies [14, 15]. However, these conditions are rarely replicated in routine African healthcare contexts, where virological failures may go undetected for a long period of time. In real-world cohorts similar to ours, such as that reported by Ismael et al. in Mozambique, the prevalence of INSTI mutations among individuals with DTG failure reached \(15 - 20\%\) [16]; in other cohorts, with different selection criteria, the rates where even higher [17]. While these findings are concerning, current evidence does not allow us to determine whether the incidence of DTG resistance is truly increasing over time, or simply more frequently identified as resistance testing becomes more accessible and widely implemented. The G118R and E138K mutations, each found in \(43.8\%\) of our resistant cases, are among the most frequently reported DTG resistance pathways in non-B subtypes, particularly subtype C, which was predominant in our sample. The relevance of G118R has been highlighted by several studies: the meta-analysis by Semengue et al. identified G118R and R263K as the most common INSTI mutations in African failures [7], while the review by Kamori and Barabona emphasized its selection in subtypes A and C, facilitated by its low fitness cost [5]. The \(\mathrm{G118R + R263K}\) combination, also observed in our study, has been associated with high-level resistance and reduced viral fitness [18], and biochemical studies [19] confirmed its preferential selection in subtype C. Our study also reinforces the strong association between a complex treatment history and resistance risk. DTG-resistant participants had a significantly longer treatment history (median 15 years) and more frequent past failures. This is consistent with Loosli et al., who reported similar patterns in a large African-European cohort [6]. Furthermore, we observed INSTI mutations even in participants who were DTG-naive or had initiated the drug while virologically suppressed. This finding are in line with reports from Mahomed et al., Fourie et al., and Mens et al., where G118R emerged under conditions of suboptimal adherence or functionally ineffective regimens [20-22]. The observed co-resistance patterns—particularly the frequent presence of M184V and K65R—highlight the threat of multi-drug resistance in individuals failing DTG-based regimens, even in the absence of PI resistance. This pattern mirrors findings from other papers who reported NNRTI and NRTI resistance in participants failing DTG-based therapy [16, 17]. Our results therefore reinforce the concern that switching to DTG without assessing virological suppression may lead to resistance selection on a background of already compromised backbones. Lastly, our findings take on special relevance considering the growing interest in long-acting therapies such as cabotegravir. The G118R mutation, also observed in our study, has been associated with reduced susceptibility to cabotegravir in vitro, raising concerns about cross-resistance [5, 23]. The editorial by Fokam et al. in Nature Medicine strongly advocates for integrating resistance testing into routine clinical care in low-income countries to avoid silent accumulation of INSTI mutations. Similarly, the review by Tao et al. emphasizes that persistent, unrecognized viremia is a key driver of resistance emergence even in ART-naive individuals, a situation reflected in our cohort [24]. ### Limitations This study has several limitations. First, due to the small number of participants included \((n = 28)\) and the fact that genotypic resistance testing was not performed systematically on all individuals with virological failure, the epidemiological value of our prevalence estimates is limited. Second, resistance testing was restricted to the integrase region only for about half of the samples, additional mutations in other regions (e.g., protease or reverse transcriptase) might have gone undetected in participants not fully sequenced. Moreover, Stanford scores were available only for a subset of individuals, precluding systematic classification of resistance levels across the full sample. Finally, data on viral load trajectories, adherence, and treatment history were incomplete for some participants, limiting the capacity to reconstruct the exact pathway leading to the emergence of resistance in each case. Despite these limitations, our study provides important early signals on the possible patterns of DTG resistance in real-world Mozambican settings and highlights the urgent need for expanded molecular surveillance. ### Public Health Implications The findings of this study could have implications for public health policy and HIV program implementation in sub-Saharan Africa. First, the emergence of DTG resistance—even among participants initiating treatment while virally suppressed—highlights the need to revise current "test-and-switch" strategies. We are aware of the effectiveness of DTG-based regimens, but we argue that virological monitoring and resistance testing should be strengthened prior to transitioning individuals to DTG-based regimens, especially in settings with a history of limited adherence or prior treatment failures. In the actual guidelines, WHO recommends the availability of genotyping testing only in context in which DTG-based regimens are not available; our results, together with other similar data, suggest the need to revise this recommendation, and make resistance testing more available on the field, in Africa, too. For these reasons, our data underscore the urgency of integrating genotypic resistance testing into national HIV guidelines and decentralizing access to such diagnostics. Establishing sentinel surveillance systems in high-prevalence areas could allow for early detection of resistance trends and inform timely changes in treatment protocols. Finally, the potential for cross-resistance to newer long-acting therapies such as cabotegravir calls for cautious and evidence-based scale-up of such interventions, considering also the extensive resistance to NNRTI typically present in individuals having failed first generation NNRTI regimens [3], that might affect the efficacy of rilpivirine (the second drug present in the long-acting regimen). Investments in molecular diagnostic capacity and targeted training of healthcare workers are essential to ensure that therapeutic innovations do not inadvertently accelerate resistance at the population level. In summary, our data confirm and expand on recent African evidence regarding DTG resistance: G118R, E138K, R263K, and L74M represent emerging mutational patterns in Mozambique, particularly among individuals with extensive treatment history, unsuppressed viral load, or prior failures. The possible spread of such mutations, even in clinically stable individuals, may have implications for the long-term sustainability of DTG-based regimens and highlights the need to implement sentinel genotypic surveillance strategies in public treatment programs. ## Conclusion This retrospective analysis describes the presence of integrase inhibitor resistance mutations among individuals with virological failure on DTG-based ART in five DREAM centers in Mozambique. Among those tested, nearly half showed evidence of resistance, with a predominance of G118R and other mutations previously associated with DTG failure in non-B subtypes. The findings reflect the need for ongoing monitoring of DTG resistance in routine programmatic settings and support the value of implementing targeted genotypic surveillance where feasible. The top 12 most common DRMs were NRTI or NNRTI mutations; 203 (61.0%) CLHIV had the most common NRTI mutation (M184V), and 143 (42.9%) had the most common NNRTI mutation (K103N). The two most common PI mutations were each found in 23 (6.9%) CLHIV (M46, V82) and 4 (1.2%) CLHIV had the most common INSTI mutation (R263).

## Discussion:

This analysis demonstrated low levels of INSTI and PI HIVDR among Ugandan CLHIV experiencing VF on first-line ART and represents the largest examination of HIVDR among CLHIV on DTG-based regimens in Sub-Saharan Africa to date. While overall rates of DRMs were high, the majority of DRMs were to NNRTIs with low rates to INSTIs and PIs. We found that CLHIV on a DTG-based regimen were least likely to have any DRMs (including non-NNRTI DRMs) compared to all other regimens, with  >95%  susceptible to DTG, LPV/r, and DRV/r. The finding of limited DTG resistance amongst children failing on DTG indicates that most children could be maintained on

their DTG-based ART with more emphasis on intensified, effective adherence support to help them achieve VS. Low rates of DRV/r resistance further support the use of DRV as an effective second-line ARV, even amongst those CLHIV failing on LPV/r. We also found that the prevalence of intermediate-to-high level resistance to ABC and AZT was relatively low ( ≤25% ) and was similar across all CLHIV, regardless of regimen at sample collection, suggesting the preferred maintenance of an ABC backbone after first-line failure. These novel HIVDR findings are important as countries develop and implement guidelines to optimize all CLHIV to first-line DTG-based regimens and determine optimal management of VF in the setting of DTG.

Consistent with existing literature is the finding that the majority (81.4%) of CLHIV with VF have at least one DRM, with a similar prevalence of NNRTI (67.6%) and NRTI (65.2%) DRMs and the most common mutations seen by class were K103N and M184V, respectively. 7,9-11  Consistent with emerging literature is the finding that the proportion of CLHIV with NNRTI DRMs does not vary between those on a PI- or NNRTI-based regimen, 12  although this study found lower rates of NNRTI DRMs among CLHIV on DTG-based regimens. Our results also showed lower rates of clinically significant resistance to 3TC among those on DTG compared to those on LPV/r, which is consistent with a small but growing body of research that suggests DTG-based regimens may be associated with lower rates of emerging HIVDR. 13,14  Similar to other smaller HIVDR studies among CLHIV on DTG-based regimens, we saw low rates of INSTI DRMs (6.6% in our study, range 5.8-18% in other studies) 14-16  and even lower rates of intermediate-to-high level resistance to DTG (4.1% in our study, range 8.9%-18% in other studies). 14-16  Though analysis methodologies differ across prior studies due to

differences in the sample population, ART at sample collection, and sampling approaches, all findings continue to demonstrate DTG efficacy and support DTG-based regimens as preferred first-line among CLHIV.

The novel findings in our study included the relatively large number of CLHIV on a DTG-based regimen with a WHO-recommended ABC+3TC backbone for CLHIV  < 30kg  compared to other HIVDR studies among CLHIV on DTG-based regimens. 14,15,17  While results from the NADIA trial have demonstrated the durability and non-inferiority of DTG when paired with a 3TC +TDF backbone even when no NRTI activity is predicted, questions remain as to whether these findings apply to CLHIV, especially those who would be optimized to DTG using a single drug substitution while maintaining their ABC+3TC backbone. 18  Our findings demonstrate that among this highly treatment experienced population of CLHIV, those with a DTG+ABC containing regimen were no more likely to have DRMs or intermediate-to-high level non-NNRTI resistance than those on DTG with a non-ABC containing backbone. Additionally, similar rates of clinically significant resistance to ABC and AZT were seen among CLHIV on a DTG-based regimen, despite higher known exposure to ABC than AZT and few children currently on AZT. While further data are needed, our findings also support the maintenance of an ABC-containing backbone among children failing LPV/r-based regimens, as we demonstrated that only  13.2%  of our population failing LPV/r may potentially benefit from switching to an AZT-containing backbone. The low rates of intermediate-to-high level resistance to TDF seen in both CLHIV on DTG and LPV/r along with results from the NADIA trial, underscore the importance of transitioning all CLHIV on DTG to a TDF-containing regimen once they reach  30kg, such as

Tenofovir/Lamivudine/Dolutegravir (TLD), which has been shown to improve VS regardless of underlying NRTI resistance.

Our study found higher rates of LPV/r resistance than previously reported among children on LPV/r-based regimens. Our findings of  14%  intermediate-to-high level resistance to LPV/r were slightly higher than the 1-10.7% reported in other studies. 12,15,19  However, our study also contributes to a small but increasingly important body of evidence which demonstrates very low rates of intermediate-to-high level resistance to DRV/r amongst children on LPV/r and DTG, indicating that DRV may be the more promising PI for second-line regimens, even in the presence of LPV/r resistance. 12,15,19

Consistent with limited available data, our study found that younger children (<5 years old) are more likely to have DRMs and intermediate-to-high level resistance. 7,19  This has important clinical implications, as these young children will need ART throughout their lives, and it will be important to prevent additional development of resistance to currently available, optimal regimens. Sample size limited our ability to further analyze resistance by regimen in these young children, but this would be an important focus of future HIVDR surveys. This analysis took place before full introduction of DTG 10mg in Uganda so further investigation into this age band is warranted as most CLHIV  <5  years will have now fully transitioned to DTG.

At the time of this analysis only  56.5%  (188/333) of CLHIV had a clinical outcome reported in their chart. Half of those with a reported outcome were maintained on their current regimen. These data suggest moderate durability of current regimens despite

high levels of HIVDR; however, minimal clinical outcome data limited our ability to draw meaningful conclusions about the impact of HIVDR testing on clinical outcomes.

An important strength of this analysis is that it is one of the first to result from HIVDR testing conducted as part of standard of care HIV treatment for all CLHIV. However, there were also several limitations, including those originating from identified gaps in programmatic HIVDR testing. Primarily, samples were only obtained from those CLHIV on ART who returned for follow up VL testing, none of whom were eligible CLHIV 16-19 years and only about half of the samples identified as eligible for inclusion were successfully traced, processed, and amplified. This limits the study's full

representativeness of the population and prevents interpretation for older adolescents.

To improve data quality in the future, improvements can be made in tracing and processing for samples eligible for HIVDR testing, as well as to better understand the factors that contributed to unsuccessful amplification for a number of the samples.

These challenges and resulting lower sample size consequently limited our ability to perform more robust analyses between and within treatment groups. Additionally, due to delays in HIVDR turnaround time and review of clinical HIVDR results, as well as gaps in documentation of clinical management using HIVDR results, we had limited ability to analyze treatment decisions' outcomes and therefore could not robustly evaluate the clinical impact of standard of care HIVDR testing. Further evaluations will be important once measures to improve turnaround time and documentation are implemented.

In conclusion, among this cohort of Ugandan CLHIV failing their first-line ART regimen, the findings of low rates of INSTI mutations and overall lower rates of clinically significant HIVDR among those on a DTG-based regimen underscores the durability of

DTG-based regimens, highlighting the importance of a rapid transition to DTG-based ART for all CLHIV, and the value of effective adherence support for those CLHIV on DTG with VF. The rates of cross-resistance seen between ABC and AZT, regardless of ART backbone at sample collection, support maintaining an ABC backbone for CLHIV  < 30  kg, at the time of DTG transition even without VL results. Further data on clinical outcomes of CLHIV with VF maintained on DTG-based regimens, especially in the presence of NRTI and INSTI resistance, could better inform guidance on the timing and necessity of a switch to a second-line regimen.


## Methods

Data for this analysis were obtained following the 2020 revision of the Uganda HIV Prevention, Care and Treatment Guidelines that recommended HIVDR testing for all children and adolescents living with HIV failing ART. In 2021, the Uganda Ministry of Health conducted standard-of-care HIVDR testing for CLHIV failing first-line ART to optimize treatment outcomes, through the support of the CDC-funded Faith-based Action for Scaling up Testing and Treatment for the Epidemic Response (FASTER) project. FASTER was implemented between 2019-2021 by Catholic Relief Services, in partnership with the Clinton Health Access Initiative, to support ministries of health in four countries (Uganda, Nigeria, Tanzania and Zambia) to improve testing and treatment of CLHIV. 8

Data for this analysis came from previously collected VL samples from children aged  ≤ 15  years of age on first-line ART enrolled in any ART-accredited health facility in Uganda whose VL sample satisfied the following criteria: (1) sample tested for VL between January and November 2021, (2) sample type was plasma (3) VF defined as

VL ≥1000 copies/mL for children on EFV or NVP or repeat VL >1000 copies/ml for children on Lopinavir/ritonavir (LPV/r) or DTG. Repeat VL refers to a VL test taken after a child with an initial unsuppressed VL has undergone intensified adherence support for at least 3 months with 3 consecutive good adherence scores. Samples from CLHIV whose prior regimen changes were made for treatment simplification or due to policy changes and not VF were classified as being on first-line ART.

A paper-based VL and HIVDR request form completed at sample collection contained details such as demographics, ART history, clinical condition, sample type and collection date for each sample. At the time of this evaluation, all VL testing was done centrally at the Central Public Health Laboratory (CPHL). CPHL had an electronic VL laboratory information system (LIMS) where the details from the VL and HIVDR request form were entered along with VL testing results, once available. LIMS data were used to filter remnant VL samples eligible for HIVDR testing based on the above inclusion criteria.

The eligible VL samples were then automatically identified by the HIV Drug Resistance Database (HIVDR Database). The HIVDR Database acts as the relay database for cross-laboratory systems interoperability. The database received eligible sample profiles from the VL LIMS and provided a user interface for referring these samples to the HIVDR laboratories. Once a sample fulfilling the inclusion criteria above was identified, it was retrieved and sent to the HIVDR laboratory at Joint Clinical Research Centre to be tested using Sanger sequencing technology if there was sufficient sample volume. Once a sample was referred to the HIVDR laboratory, clinicians received email notifications from the HIVDR Database to upload their clients' social, psychosocial, and

medical profiles into the database. When the HIVDR results were available, the HIVDR laboratory systems automatically pushed the results into the HIVDR Database, from which clinicians and experts could review the results and make ART recommendations. Once individual treatment decisions were made and documented, these clinical recommendations were also uploaded into the HIVDR database.

The data presented in this work were therefore a combination of the routine data inputs by clinicians, VL and HIVDR laboratories, and drug resistance review committees, all aggregated within the HIVDR Database. These data were stored in a relational database and were extracted, cleaned, and transformed using the Structured Query Language and exported as a Comma Separated Value database for further cleaning and analysis.

The analytic dataset of demographic data and HIVDR information for sampled specimens were retrieved from the HIVDR Database in March 2022. HIV drug resistance mutations (DRMs) and drug susceptibility profiles were generated using Stanford University's HIVdb algorithm (version 9.0) (https://hivdb.stanford.edu/hivdb). All analyses were conducted using Stata 18 statistical software (StataCorp LLC, College Station, TX). Frequencies of DRMs were calculated overall and stratified by drug class of the mutation, including mutations against NRTIs, NNRTIs, protease inhibitors (PIs), and integrase inhibitors (INSTIs). The frequencies of individual DRMs were also calculated overall and stratified by regimen at sample collection. Mutations and resistance were classified as non-NNRTI if they were identified in any of the following drug classes; NRTIs, PIs, and/or INSTIs. Individuals were considered to have clinically significant HIVDR if their drug susceptibility profile revealed intermediate-to-high level

drug resistance to one or more of the following individual ARVs: DTG, abacavir (ABC), zidovudine (AZT), tenofovir disoproxil fumarate (TDF), lamivudine (3TC), LPV/r, darunavir (DRV), EFV, or NVP. All calculations were estimated overall, and stratified by regimen at blood sample collection, and by previous exposure to the child's known historical treatment regimens.

To determine possible correlates of DRMs and HIVDR, associations with various demographic and clinical factors were determined using chi square tests. P-values  < 0.05  were considered statistically significant. The outcomes of interest were presence of any DRMs and presence of intermediate-to-high level drug resistance to any non-NNRTI ARVs. Demographic and clinical variables explored included sex, age category, duration of time on ART, reported level of adherence to ART (good, fair, or poor), VL category at sample collection (defined as VL  < 10,000, VL 10,000-100,000, and VL>100,000), and regimen at sample collection. A standardized behavioral questionnaire was completed for participants as part of their clinical care; correlates of DRMs and drug susceptibility were also explored for a variety of social susceptibility factors. To better characterize children on optimized ART, demographic factors were described for children on DTG-based regimens by their specific NRTI backbone. Among these children, presence of DRMs and non-NNRTI drug resistance was compared between children on DTG+ABC regimens compared to other DTG-based regimens using chi square tests.

Frequencies were also calculated for the clinical recommendations reported after HIVDR testing, both overall and stratified by drug class of DRMs. The potential clinical recommendations included maintaining on current regimen, substituting with another

ARV within the first-line, switching to another drug class or second-line regimen, or pending if clinical recommendations were not noted.

This activity was reviewed by CDC, deemed not research, and was conducted consistent with applicable federal law and CDC policy. 1

## Results

Between January and November 2021, 648 VL samples from 164 sites met the inclusion criteria. A total of 428 (66.0%) samples were retrieved from the sample biorepository and sent to the HIVDR lab for testing; 128 (19.8%) did not meet the Sanger testing criteria due to low sample volume or other factors. Of the 428 samples referred for HIVDR testing, 333 (77.8%) samples were successfully tested while 95 (22.2%) samples failed to amplify.

Among the 333 CLHIV with successful sample amplification, 61 (18.3%) were aged 1-4 years, 79 (23.7%) aged 5-9 years, 89 (26.7%) aged 10-12 years, and 104 (31.2%) aged 13-15 years (Table 1). There were 101 (30.3%) CLHIV taking ART for less than five years, 104 (31.2%) taking ART 5-9 years, and 128 (38.4%) taking ART 10 or more years. At the time of sample collection, 122 (36.6%) CLHIV were taking a DTG-based regimen, 136 (40.8%) were taking an LPV/r-based regimen, and 74 (22.2%) were taking either an EFV- or NVP-based regimen. Among the 122 CLHIV on DTG-based regimens, the median age was 13 years (interquartile range [IQR]=11-14); 54 (44.2%) were on regimens with an ABC/3TC backbone, 65 (53.3%) had a TDF/3TC backbone, and 3

(2.5%) had an AZT/3TC backbone. The median age in years for these subgroups was 12 for ABC (IQR=10-13), 13 for TDF (IQR=12-14), and 9 for AZT (IQR=2-10).

Of the 333 CLHIV, 271 (81.4%) had any DRMs (Table 2); 10 (3.0%) had any INSTI DRMs; 39 (11.7%) had any PI DRMs; 217 (65.2%) had any NRTI DRMs; and 225 (67.6%) had any NNRTI DRMs. Many CLHIV had DRMs against multiple classes of ARTs: 184 (55.3%) had DRMs against 2 classes and 36 (10.8%) had DRMs against 3 classes. These frequencies varied by regimen at sample collection (Table 2) and history of ARV exposure (Table 3). Of note, children on DTG at sample collection had lower frequencies of DRMs for all drug classes except INSTIs. Rates of DRMs against INSTIs among children on DTG were low (6.6%, 8/122), though were twice as common in these children when compared to the overall sample (3.0%, 10/333) and about 6 times more common when compared to CLHIV not on DTG at sample collection (0.95%, 10/333). The most common individual DRMs are presented in Table 4. The top 12 most common DRMs were NRTI or NNRTI mutations; 203 (61.0%) CLHIV had the most common NRTI mutation (M184V), and 143 (42.9%) had the most common NNRTI mutation (K103N). The two most common PI mutations were each found in 23 (6.9%) CLHIV (M46, V82) and 4 (1.2%) CLHIV had the most common INSTI mutation (R263).

Drug susceptibility analysis revealed that the majority of CLHIV (78.7%, 262/333) had clinically significant resistance (intermediate-to-high level drug resistance) to at least one ARV, including: DTG (1.8%), LPV (9.6%), DRV (1.8%), NVP (67.0%), EFV (66.1%), 3TC (61.0%), ABC (25.5%), and AZT (19.2%) (Table 2). Similar to DRMs, individual drug susceptibility varied by regimen at sample collection (Table 2) and history of ARV exposure (Table 3). CLHIV on DTG-based regimens at the time of sample collection

had the lowest prevalence of any intermediate-to-high level drug resistance at  69.7%, with resistance to EFV (58.2%) and NVP (59.8%) most frequent (Table 2). Of the 122 CLHIV failing on DTG, intermediate-to-high-level resistance was lower for other ARVs, including for: DTG (4.1%), LPV (4.1%), DRV (0.8%), ABC (21.3%), AZT (18%), and TDF (6.6%) (Table 2). Among 136 children failing on LPV/r, intermediate-to-high level resistance included: LPV/r (14.0%), DTG (0.7%), DRV (1.5%), ABC (27.2%), AZT (14.0%), and TDF (8.8%) (Table 2). All those with AZT resistance were also resistant to ABC leaving only 18 (13.2%) of those failing LPV/r with intermediate-high level ABC resistance and without similar AZT resistance. On average, intermediate-to-high level resistance to a particular drug tended to be higher in CLHIV on a regimen containing that drug at sample collection compared to the level of resistance to that drug among all sampled CLHIV. For instance, resistance to DTG was approximately eight times as high among CLHIV currently taking DTG (4.1%) compared to CLHIV not taking DTG (0.5%) [chi squared  p = 0.02 ] and approximately 2 times higher to AZT (32.1% compared to 16.8%,  p = 0.01 ) and LPV (14.0% compared to 6.6%,  p = 0.02 ) for those on regimens containing these drugs, respectively. However, notably, this pattern was not seen for ABC (Table 2).

In bivariate analyses, similar patterns were seen for presence of DRMs and presence of non-NNRTI intermediate-to-high level drug resistance (Table 5). Overall, the youngest CLHIV were more likely to have DRMs  ( p = 0.02 )  and were more likely to have any non-NNRTI resistance  ( p = 0.01 ). CLHIV on DTG-based regimens at sample collection were less likely to have both DRMs  ( p = 0.007 )  or non-NNRTI resistance  ( p = 0.02 )  compared to those on non-DTG-based regimens, and CLHIV on LPV/r-based regimens were more

likely to have both DRMs  ( p = 0.04 )  and non-NNRTI resistance  ( p = 0.05 )  compared to those on non-LPV/r-based regimens. Among CLHIV on a DTG-based regimen at sample collection, the 54 (44.3%) children with an ABC-containing backbone were no more likely to have clinically relevant mutations  ( p = 0.9 )  or non-NNRTI resistance  ( p = 0.5 )  compared to children on a DTG-based regimen with a different backbone. No relationship was seen for either DRMs or intermediate-to-high level resistance by sex, duration on ART, adherence score, VL at sample collection (Table 5), or most social susceptibility factors (Table S1).

At the time of data collection, almost half of CLHIV in the database (N=145, 43%) had no information on clinical recommendations after HIVDR testing (Table S2). However, among those with clinical recommendations, 94 (28.2%) were maintained on their current regimen, 55 (16.5%) were switched to another drug class, and 39 (11.7%) had a single drug substitution.

## Discussion:

This analysis demonstrated low levels of INSTI and PI HIVDR among Ugandan CLHIV experiencing VF on first-line ART and represents the largest examination of HIVDR among CLHIV on DTG-based regimens in Sub-Saharan Africa to date. While overall rates of DRMs were high, the majority of DRMs were to NNRTIs with low rates to INSTIs and PIs. We found that CLHIV on a DTG-based regimen were least likely to have any DRMs (including non-NNRTI DRMs) compared to all other regimens, with  >95%  susceptible to DTG, LPV/r, and DRV/r. The finding of limited DTG resistance amongst children failing on DTG indicates that most children could be maintained on

their DTG-based ART with more emphasis on intensified, effective adherence support to help them achieve VS. Low rates of DRV/r resistance further support the use of DRV as an effective second-line ARV, even amongst those CLHIV failing on LPV/r. We also found that the prevalence of intermediate-to-high level resistance to ABC and AZT was relatively low ( ≤25% ) and was similar across all CLHIV, regardless of regimen at sample collection, suggesting the preferred maintenance of an ABC backbone after first-line failure. These novel HIVDR findings are important as countries develop and implement guidelines to optimize all CLHIV to first-line DTG-based regimens and determine optimal management of VF in the setting of DTG.

Consistent with existing literature is the finding that the majority (81.4%) of CLHIV with VF have at least one DRM, with a similar prevalence of NNRTI (67.6%) and NRTI (65.2%) DRMs and the most common mutations seen by class were K103N and M184V, respectively. 7,9-11  Consistent with emerging literature is the finding that the proportion of CLHIV with NNRTI DRMs does not vary between those on a PI- or NNRTI-based regimen, 12  although this study found lower rates of NNRTI DRMs among CLHIV on DTG-based regimens. Our results also showed lower rates of clinically significant resistance to 3TC among those on DTG compared to those on LPV/r, which is consistent with a small but growing body of research that suggests DTG-based regimens may be associated with lower rates of emerging HIVDR. 13,14  Similar to other smaller HIVDR studies among CLHIV on DTG-based regimens, we saw low rates of INSTI DRMs (6.6% in our study, range 5.8-18% in other studies) 14-16  and even lower rates of intermediate-to-high level resistance to DTG (4.1% in our study, range 8.9%-18% in other studies). 14-16  Though analysis methodologies differ across prior studies due to

differences in the sample population, ART at sample collection, and sampling approaches, all findings continue to demonstrate DTG efficacy and support DTG-based regimens as preferred first-line among CLHIV.

The novel findings in our study included the relatively large number of CLHIV on a DTG-based regimen with a WHO-recommended ABC+3TC backbone for CLHIV  < 30kg  compared to other HIVDR studies among CLHIV on DTG-based regimens. 14,15,17  While results from the NADIA trial have demonstrated the durability and non-inferiority of DTG when paired with a 3TC +TDF backbone even when no NRTI activity is predicted, questions remain as to whether these findings apply to CLHIV, especially those who would be optimized to DTG using a single drug substitution while maintaining their ABC+3TC backbone. 18  Our findings demonstrate that among this highly treatment experienced population of CLHIV, those with a DTG+ABC containing regimen were no more likely to have DRMs or intermediate-to-high level non-NNRTI resistance than those on DTG with a non-ABC containing backbone. Additionally, similar rates of clinically significant resistance to ABC and AZT were seen among CLHIV on a DTG-based regimen, despite higher known exposure to ABC than AZT and few children currently on AZT. While further data are needed, our findings also support the maintenance of an ABC-containing backbone among children failing LPV/r-based regimens, as we demonstrated that only  13.2%  of our population failing LPV/r may potentially benefit from switching to an AZT-containing backbone. The low rates of intermediate-to-high level resistance to TDF seen in both CLHIV on DTG and LPV/r along with results from the NADIA trial, underscore the importance of transitioning all CLHIV on DTG to a TDF-containing regimen once they reach  30kg, such as

Tenofovir/Lamivudine/Dolutegravir (TLD), which has been shown to improve VS regardless of underlying NRTI resistance.

Our study found higher rates of LPV/r resistance than previously reported among children on LPV/r-based regimens. Our findings of  14%  intermediate-to-high level resistance to LPV/r were slightly higher than the 1-10.7% reported in other studies. 12,15,19  However, our study also contributes to a small but increasingly important body of evidence which demonstrates very low rates of intermediate-to-high level resistance to DRV/r amongst children on LPV/r and DTG, indicating that DRV may be the more promising PI for second-line regimens, even in the presence of LPV/r resistance. 12,15,19

Consistent with limited available data, our study found that younger children (<5 years old) are more likely to have DRMs and intermediate-to-high level resistance. 7,19  This has important clinical implications, as these young children will need ART throughout their lives, and it will be important to prevent additional development of resistance to currently available, optimal regimens.
